'''''Rubus armeniacus''''', the '''giant blackberry''',<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web |title=Giant Blackberry ''Rubus armeniacus'' Focke |website=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.mnf |access-date=2026-08-06}}</ref> '''Armenian blackberry''',<ref name="e896">{{cite web |title=Armenian blackberry ''Rubus armeniacus'' |url=https://www.oregon.gov/oda/Documents/Publications/Weeds/ArmeniaBlackberryProfile.pdf |access-date=2026-08-06}}</ref> or sometimes, misleadingly, "Himalayan blackberry",<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RUAR9|taxon=Rubus armeniacus|access-date=24 October 2015}}</ref> is a species of ''[[Rubus]]'' in the [[blackberry]] group ''Rubus'' subgenus ''Rubus'' series ''Discolores'' (P.J. Müll.) Focke. It is native to [[Armenia]] and northwestern [[Iran]], and widely [[Invasive species|invasive]] elsewhere.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=''Rubus armeniacus'' Focke |website=Plants of the World Online |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:735202-1 |access-date=2026-08-06}}</ref> Both its scientific name and origin have been the subject of much confusion.

It is known for its extreme vigour and tendency to spread rapidly over disturbed areas. It is considered an [[invasive species]] and a [[noxious weed]] in many regions, but is or was also widely cultivated for its edible fruit; this is large and sweet when ripe, and is one of the most popular blackberries.<ref name="PlantAtlas"/> Its history of discovery and introduction into cultivation are poorly documented; its first definite cultivation was in Germany by 1889,<ref name="PlantAtlas"/> but probably earlier, in 1835, under the name "''Rubus fruticosus fr. maximo'' Booth".<ref name=ben/>{{efn|This is nearly 40 years before the species was described, so its application to this species is open to some uncertainty}}

==Description==
[[File:Korina 2011-08-08 Rubus armeniacus 15.jpg|thumb|left|First year stem with stout prickles]]
[[File:Korina 2011-08-02 Rubus armeniacus 2.jpg|thumb|left|First year stem with leaves with five leaflets]]
''Rubus armeniacus'' is a [[perennial]] plant that bears [[Biennial plant|biennial]] stems ("canes") from the perennial root system. In its first year a new stem grows vigorously to its full length of {{Convert|4–10|m}}, trailing along the ground or arching up to 4 m high. The stem is stout, up to 2–3 cm diameter at the base, and green; it is polygonal (usually hexagonal) in cross-section, with stout [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|prickles]] up to 1.5 cm long forming along the ribs. The canes can turn more red/purple if they are exposed to bright sunlight. This is common in the summer.

The [[leaves]] on first-year shoots are {{Convert|7–20|cm|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} long, [[Leaf shape|palmately compound]] with either three or more commonly five leaflets. The leaflets are moderately serrated. Flowers are not produced on first-year shoots. In its second year, the stem does not grow longer, but produces several side shoots, which bear smaller leaves with three leaflets (rarely a single leaflet). These leaflets are oval-acute, dark green above and pale to whitish below, with a toothed margin, and snaring, hooked thorns along the midrib on the underside. Both first- and second-year shoots are spiny, with short, stout, curved, sharp prickles. Mature plants form a tangle of dense arching stems, the branches rooting from the node tip when they reach the ground.<ref name=usfs>Francis, J.K. (2003). ''Rubus discolor'' Weihe & Nees. [http://www.fs.fed.us/global/iitf/pdf/shrubs/Rubus%20discolor.pdf pdf file]</ref> The [[flower]]s are produced in late spring and early summer on [[panicle]]s of 3–20 together on the tips of the second-year side shoots, each flower 2–2.5 cm diameter with five white or pale pink [[petal]]s. The flowers are [[:simple:Flowering plant sexuality|bisexual]] (perfect) containing both male and female reproductive structures.<ref>{{cite book |title=Flora of North America: North of Mexico |author=Flora of North America editorial committee |date=2005 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780195222111 |oclc=469452032}}</ref> The [[fruit]] in botanical terminology is not a [[Berry (botany)|berry]], but an [[aggregate fruit]] of numerous [[drupe]]lets. It is 1.2–2 cm diameter, ripening black or dark purple.

==Taxonomy==
Both the scientific name and the species' origin have been the subject of much confusion, with much of the literature referring to it as either ''Rubus procerus'' or ''Rubus discolor'', and often mistakenly citing its origin as western European.<ref name=ben>Ceska, A. (1999). ''Rubus armeniacus'' – a correct name for Himalayan Blackberries ''Botanical Electronic News'' 230. Available [http://www.ou.edu/cas/botany-micro/ben/ben230.html online].</ref><ref name=fnwe>Flora of NW Europe: [http://wbd.etibioinformatics.nl/bis/flora.php?menuentry=soorten&id=2618 ''Rubus armeniacus'']</ref><ref>University of British Columbia Botany Photo of the Day: [http://www.ubcbotanicalgarden.org/potd/2005/07/rubus_armeniacu.php 21 July 2005: ''Rubus armeniacus'']</ref> The ''[[Flora of North America]]'', published in 2014, considers the taxonomy unsettled, and tentatively uses the older name ''[[Rubus bifrons]]'',<ref>{{citation |chapter-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242417158 |chapter=''Rubus bifrons'' Vest, Steyermärk. Z. 3: 163. 1821 |author1=Lawrence A. Alice |author2=Douglas H. Goldman |author3=James A. Macklin |author4=Gerry Moore |name-list-style=amp |title=Flora of North America online |volume=9 |year=2014}}</ref> but this is now treated by the ''[[Plants of the World Online]]'' database as a separate, central European species.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Rubus bifrons'' Vest |website=Plants of the World Online |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:60449596-2 |access-date=2026-08-06}}</ref>

==Ecology==
The fleshy growing cane tips contain the [[antifeedant]] compounds, [[2-heptanol]] and [[methyl salicylate]] at higher concentrations than mature leaves. At the concentration found in the growing cane tips, 2-heptanol is a banana slug (''[[Ariolimax columbianus]]'') antifeedant. The lack of phytophagous insects observed on the growing cane tips is likely due to the presence of methyl salicylate. This compound is a known [[aphid]] repellant and has been shown to attract predators in response to insect herbivory.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wood |first=William F. |title=Banana slug antifeedant in the growing cane tips of Himalayan Berry Rubus armeniacus |journal=Biochemical Systematics and Ecology |volume=41 |pages=126–129 |year=2012 |doi=10.1016/j.bse.2011.12.029|bibcode=2012BioSE..41..126W }}</ref>

=== As an invasive species ===
[[File:Rubus armeniacus Massenbestand.jpg|thumb|left|''R. armeniacus'' covering a field in Germany]]

==== Spread ====
[[Luther Burbank]], who coined the misleading name "Himalayan", introduced ''R. armeniacus'' to North America in 1885 in [[Santa Rosa, California]], using seeds that he imported from India.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Burbank |first1=Luther |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/115372 |title=Luther Burbank, his methods and discoveries and their practical application |last2=Whitson |first2=John |last3=John |first3=Robert |last4=Williams |first4=Henry Smith |last5=Society |first5=Luther Burbank |date=1914 |publisher=Luther Burbank Press |volume=6 |location=London |pages=27–30}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Luther Burbank {{!}} Encyclopedia.com |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/science-and-technology/horticulture-biographies/luther-burbank |access-date=2022-12-12 |website=www.encyclopedia.com}}</ref> The species thrived in its new environment, notably for the large amount of berries it produced. By 1915, it was widely grown and cultivated in the United States.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Burbank |first1=Luther |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/54007 |title=Luther Burbank, his methods and discoveries and their practical application |last2=Whitson |first2=John |last3=John |first3=Robert |last4=Williams |first4=Henry Smith |last5=Society |first5=Luther Burbank |date=1914 |publisher=Luther Burbank Press |location=London}}</ref> It soon [[Escaped plant|escaped from cultivation]], and became an [[invasive species]] in most of the temperate world and the U.S. Pacific Coast by 1945.<ref name="ben" /><ref name="fnwe" /><ref name=":0">USDA Plant Profile: [https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=RUAR9 ''Rubus armeniacus'']</ref><ref>Multiple sources:
* {{cite web |last=Hoshovsky |first=Marc |date=1989 |title=ELEMENT STEWARDSHIP ABSTRACT for Rubus discolor, (Rubus procerus) |url=https://www.invasive.org/gist/esadocs/documnts/rubuarm.pdf}}
* National list of naturalised invasive and potentially invasive garden plants (Australia) [http://awsassets.wwf.org.au/downloads/sp092_list_invasive_garden_plant_4apr06.pdf pdf file]
* {{cite journal | url=http://ir.library.oregonstate.edu/concern/open_educational_resources/0r967408h |first=Max |last=Bennett |title=Managing Himalayan blackberry in western Oregon riparian areas |website=OSU Extension Catalog |date=August 2006 |access-date=2022-07-04 |s2cid=128858520 |hdl=1957/20389 |publisher=[[Oregon State University Extension Service]] |id=[https://catalog.extension.oregonstate.edu/sites/catalog/files/project/pdf/em8894.pdf PDF] |quote=It escaped cultivation and has since invaded a variety of sites, including low-elevation streamside areas throughout the Pacific Northwest. Listed as a noxious weed in Oregon, Himalayan blackberry rapidly occupies disturbed areas, is very difficult to eradicate once established, and tends to out-compete native vegetation. For those trying to restore or enhance native streamside vegetation, Himalayan blackberry control is a major problem.}}</ref> It is listed as an invasive species in the U.S. State of Missouri and prohibited in the U.S. state of Wisconsin.<ref>{{cite web |last1=National Plant Data Team |title=Rubus armeniacus Focke |url=https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=RUAR9 |website=USDA Plants Database |publisher=USDA, NRCS |access-date=29 October 2024}}</ref> Because it is so hard to contain, it quickly gets out of control, with birds and other animals eating the fruit and then spreading the seeds.<ref>[http://www.invasive.org/gist/moredocs/rubarm01.pdf The Nature Conservancy, Controlling Himalayan Blackberry in the Pacific Northwest by Jonathan Soll]</ref> It is highly flammable and a common [[ladder fuel]] for wildfires,<ref>{{cite web |last=Kilders |first=Lisa |date=2020-08-24 |title=Protect Your Forest From Fire |url=https://conservationdistrict.org/2020/protect-your-forest-from-fire.html |access-date=2021-08-25 |website=Clackamas SWCD |language=en-US}}</ref> due to the litter and dead canes produced by the plant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gaire |first1=R |last2=Astley |last3=C |first3=Upadhyaya |last4=M |first4=ClementsD |last5=BargenM |date=2015-05-01 |title=The Biology of Canadian Weeds. 154. Himalayan blackberry |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/abs/10.4141/cjps-2014-402 |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |volume=95 |issue=3 |pages=557–570 |doi=10.4141/cjps-2014-402|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Fire-Resistant Landscaping {{!}} Veneta Oregon |url=https://www.venetaoregon.gov/publicsafety/page/fire-resistant-landscaping |access-date=2021-08-25 |website=www.venetaoregon.gov}}</ref>

It is especially established west of the [[Cascade Range|Cascades]] in the American Pacific Northwest<ref name=":1">{{cite web |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/shrub/rubarm/all.html |title=Rubus armeniacus |website=www.fs.fed.us |access-date=2019-04-19}}</ref> and in parts of southern British Columbia along the coast, in the [[Lower Mainland]], and throughout [[Vancouver Island]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Invasive Species Council of BC |date=March 2019 |title=Himalayan Blackberry |url=https://bcinvasives.ca/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Himalayan_Blackberry_Factsheet_20190220.pdf}}</ref> It does well in riparian zones due to the abundance of other species in these areas, which allows it to go relatively unnoticed until it has had a chance to establish itself.<ref name=":0" /> Unlike other invasive species, this plant can easily establish itself and continue to spread in ecosystems that have not experienced a disturbance.<ref name=":1" />

The plant itself develops large root systems, allowing it to find water from other sources than just the immediate area. It can also hold onto water in its canes, allowing it to thrive more than other plants during dry seasons or droughts.<ref name=":02">{{cite journal |last=Caplan |first=Joshua |date=2009-01-30 |title=The Role of Water and Other Resources in the Invasion of Rubus Armeniacus in Pacific Northwest Ecosystems |url=https://pdxscholar.library.pdx.edu/open_access_etds/5946 |journal=Dissertations and Theses |doi=10.15760/etd.7816 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Himalayan blackberries grow very well in sandy, well-drained soil with a lot of natural light, even if the soil is lacking in nutrients.<ref name=":12">{{cite journal |last1=Caplan |first1=Joshua S. |last2=Yeakley |first2=J. Alan |date=2006 |title=Rubus armeniacus (Himalayan blackberry) Occurrence and Growth in Relation to Soil and Light Conditions in Western Oregon |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228344920 |journal=Northwest Science |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=9–17}}</ref> All of the Himalayan blackberry's adaptations to grow in these conditions continue to make it a difficult plant to remove and an invasive species. ''R. armeniacus'' is able to survive during drought periods because of their extensive root systems. Not only are their roots spread out over a wide area, they also can go very deep underground, allowing them to reach water most smaller plants and shrubs would not reach.<ref name=":12" /> They also store more water in their canes that act like a water reservoir.<ref name=":02"/> This added water also allows them to release oxygen and take in more CO<sub>2</sub> without fearing major losses of water. Since they store water in their canes and roots, they have excess water ready for use or for loss when opening their stomata.<ref name=":02"/>

==== Management ====
[[File:Korina 2011-08-10 Rubus armeniacus.jpg|thumb|An example of the fruit, showing both ripe and unripe (green then red) fruit.]]
[[File:Rubus armeniacus (55026908015).jpg|thumb|Remnants of berries during winter near [[Frederikshavn]], Denmark]]
The plant's many means of asexual reproduction make it among the most difficult to control weeds in a home garden or small property management context. Cutting the canes to the ground, or burning thickets of ''R. armeniacus'' are ineffective removal strategies. The best practices for removal include digging up the rhizomes and connecting underground structures, and herbicides.<ref name=":0" /> Broken roots can resprout, making manual removal difficult. 

The plant rarely impedes large-scale construction or agricultural practices, since tillage, cutting, and other means of mechanical removal are sufficient to destroy a single generation of plants.<ref>[https://www.nwcb.wa.gov/images/weeds/Rubu_armeniacus.pdf University of Washington]</ref>

==Cultivation==

===Fruit crop===
The species was probably introduced to Europe in 1835 and to Australia and North America in 1885. It is valued for its edible fruit, similar to that of common [[blackberries]] (e.g. ''[[Rubus fruticosus]]'') but larger and sweeter, making it a more attractive species for both domestic and commercial fruit production. The immature fruit is smaller, red, and hard with a much more sour taste. The [[cultivar]]s ''Himalayan Giant'' and ''Theodore Reimers'' are commonly planted.<ref name=ben/><ref name=fnwe/> ''Rubus armeniacus'' was used in the development of the [[marionberry]] cultivar of blackberry.<ref name=":0" />

=== Cover ===
When established for several years and if left alone, ''Rubus armeniacus'' can grow into a large cluster of canes. These thickets can provide good nesting grounds for birds, and help to provide places to rest/hide for other larger mammals, such as rabbits, squirrels, and beavers.<ref name=":1" /> While areas with ''R. armeniacus'' provide good sources for bird nests, birds in regions where it is a non-native invasive species may prefer areas with more natural/native plants when given the option.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Library and Archives |date=2022-09-01 |title=Item – Theses Canada |url=https://library-archives.canada.ca/eng/services/services-libraries/theses/Pages/item.aspx?idNumber=758060862 |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=library-archives.canada.ca}}</ref>
